We spent €100 of promo credit on a LinkedIn boost targeting 130K Greek owners and founders. The results beat the platform average by 9x — here's exactly what worked.

The numbers:
→ 4,237 impressions
→ 176 clicks at €0.51 each
→ 4.15% CTR — LinkedIn's sponsored median is ~0.44%
→ 308 engagements, a 7.27% engagement rate

The targeting discipline behind it, straight from LinkedIn's own boost playbook:

1. Pick ONE clear buyer. We went for current job titles — owners, founders, CEOs — in Greece. Not "business people". One buyer.
2. Exclude hard. Filter out titles, industries and company sizes that will never buy. Exclusions matter as much as inclusions.
3. Stay in the 50K–500K sweet spot. Under 10K barely delivers; over 500K burns budget on the wrong people. Ours sat at ~130K.

And the honest part nobody advertises: we set a hard lifetime cap and a hard end date. When the credit ran out, we stopped — the account still overshot by €6.28, which is exactly why caps matter.

Cheap impressions aren't the win. Reaching the right 130K is.

Nobody warns you about this part.

You set up the perfect posting schedule. You batch content on Sunday. Furthermore, you feel organized.

Then Tuesday hits. The pipeline breaks at 11pm. A token dies mid-queue. A model endpoint drops mid-render.

And you spend your night fixing infra instead of creating.

I know. I just lived it. This week alone:

- A kernel update sat pending for days. Services got slow.
- A TikTok audit got bounced. The demo video was too thin.
- One checkbox nearly pushed empty drafts to 3 platforms.
- A mail server restart at 2am killed the morning digest.
- A disk filled up, and the backup job died without a sound.

Here is the part nobody posts about.

Automation does not remove work. It moves work to the edges. Tokens expire. Audits bounce. Limits bite. Edge cases pile up fast.

The fix is not more tools. The fix is self-healing.

Watchdogs restart dead jobs. Scripts clean up before disks fill. Alerts fire only when a human is needed. Logs tell you what broke before your audience does.

My stack still breaks. I just stopped being the one who has to notice.

That is the real win. Not zero failures. Zero silent failures.

Every service now reports its own health. Every cron job leaves a trace. Every failed unit gets one auto retry before I ever hear about it.

So ask yourself one thing. Does your system tell you when it is sick? Or do your followers find out first?

Self-hosted. Self-healing. Self-reporting. That is the bar now.

What was your most expensive silent failure?

Pod status at 23:40 on a Tuesday. Everything green, nothing managed by anyone else.

There were weeks when this same dashboard was red — a bad image, a stuck sync job, a scheduled job that fired twice. Each one got fixed and stayed fixed.

That feeling when the checks pass and nobody paged you: that's why I self-host.
